abstract:
All parallel algorithms for directed reachability and shortest paths crucially rely on efficient shortcut constructions. These constructions find directed paths and shortcut them by adding edges, with the goal to reduce the diameter of the graph. A long sequence of works has studied (efficient) shortcut constructions as well as impossibility results on the best diameter and therefore the best parallelism that can be achieved via this approach.
This paper introduces a new conceptual tool for this line of research in the form of a simple and natural structural criterion: A shortcut H for a graph G is certified if for any shortcut edge (u, v) ∈ H, there exists a vertex w such that the edges (u, w) and (w, v) are also in G ∪ H.
We show that this criterion captures constructiveness in the following sense: A shortcut H can be constructed in t time by repeatedly spending 𝓁 time on shortcutting a path of length 𝓁, if and only if, there exists a certified shortcut H' ⊇ H of size Õ(t). Furthermore, all known shortcut constructions with efficient algorithms can be extended to produce certified shortcuts of size Õ(m). On the other hand, for shortcut constructions for which attempts to find efficient implementations have failed, we can show that this is impossible.
We also obtain stronger diameter lower bounds for certified shortcuts and hopsets. For example, no certified shortcut construction with almost-linear size can reduce a graph’s diameter below n^{1/4-o(1)}. This seems to be the best bound one can hope for with current techniques.

      Abstract
All parallel algorithms for directed reachability and shortest paths crucially rely on efficient shortcut
constructions. These constructions find directed paths and shortcut them by adding edges, with the
goal to reduce the diameter of the graph. A long sequence of works has studied (efficient) shortcut
constructions as well as impossibility results on the best diameter and therefore the best parallelism
that can be achieved via this approach.

and natural structural criterion: A shortcut H for a graph G is certified if for any shortcut edge
(u, v) ∈ H, there exists a vertex w such that the edges (u, w) and (w, v) are also in G ∪ H.
    We show that this criterion captures constructiveness in the following sense: A shortcut H can
be constructed in t time by repeatedly spending ℓ time on shortcutting a path of length ℓ, if and
only if, there exists a certified shortcut H ′ ⊇ H of size Õ(t). Furthermore, all known shortcut
constructions with efficient algorithms can be extended to produce certified shortcuts of size Õ(m).
On the other hand, for shortcut constructions for which attempts to find efficient implementations
have failed, we can show that this is impossible.
    We also obtain stronger diameter lower bounds for certified shortcuts and hopsets. For example,
no certified shortcut construction with almost-linear size can reduce a graph’s diameter below
n1/4−o(1) . This seems to be the best bound one can hope for with current techniques.

         1     Introduction
        One of the central and long-standing open problems in parallel computing is computing
        shortest paths or even just directed reachability. Despite the presence of simple and efficient
        algorithms in the sequential setting, designing parallel algorithms that are both work-efficient
        and have low depth is notoriously difficult. So far, the best such algorithm, due to [12], has
        depth n1/2+o(1) .
            The critical ingredient and primary idea powering all known parallel algorithms are
        shortcuts. On a directed acyclic graph (DAG) G = (V, E) of diameter D, a standard parallel
        breadth-first search algorithm can resolve reachability with almost-linear work and depth
        Õ(D). However, the input DAG could have a diameter as large as Θ(n). Computing a
        shortcut to reduce the diameter can drastically improve the depth of the breadth-first search.

        ▶ Definition 1. A shortcut H for a DAG G is a subset of edges from the transitive closure
        of G.

        Suppose that there exists a shortcut H of size |H| = m1+o(1) that can be constructed
        with almost-linear work and depth D′ , such that, the graph G ∪ H has diameter D. This
        immediately implies an efficient algorithm for directed reachability with almost-linear work
        and depth Õ(D + D′ ) – simply compute the shortcut H and run a breadth-first search on
        G ∪ H. Conversely, if no (efficiently computable) shortcuts with low diameters exist in general
        graphs, then this poses a limitation on the best depth achievable by any algorithm following
        this shortcut-based approach, and therefore a severe barrier for improving the current state
        of the art.
            A major advantage of studying shortcuts is that they are purely combinatorial structures,
        independent of any computation model. This, combined with the above connection, makes it
        possible to apply graph-theoretic and purely structural results to give strong evidence about
        parallel computations.
            A long line of work has studied the (non-)existence of shortcuts with low diameters. The
        state of the art lower bound due to [10] shows that O(m)-size shortcuts cannot in general
        reduce the diameter of a graph below Ω(n2/9 ), while on the upper bound side, O(n)-size
        shortcuts reducing diameter to O(n1/3 ) are known to exist for all graphs [14, 2].
            Similar approaches have also been extended to hopsets, which are generalizations of
        shortcuts that reduce the number of edges on shortest paths, instead of arbitrary paths,
        while preserving distances, not just connectivity.

        ▶ Definition 2. A hopset H for a graph G with positive edge lengths is a set of edges such
        that distG (u, v) = distG∪H (u, v) for every pair of vertices u, v.

        A hopset H for G is said to have hopbound β if for any pair of vertices u, v, where u can
        reach v, G ∪ H contains a shortest (u, v)-path with at most β edges. So far, the best known
        hopset construction remains the one produced by the folklore algorithm [19, 4], obtaining a
        hopbound of O(n1/2 ) by adding O(n) edges. For lower bounds, [10] shows O(m)-size hopsets
        cannot in general obtain a hopbound of o(n2/7 ).
           A more detailed discussion on prior work is provided in Section 1.2.


        1.1    Our Results
        This paper introduces new conceptual tools to study the structure of shortcuts that can be
        efficiently produced by a large and natural family of shortcut construction algorithms.

    There are two aspects in which existential results on shortcuts are non-constructive.
Firstly, how does one efficiently decide which node pairs to shortcut? Secondly, how can one
be convinced that an edge (u, v) is a valid shortcut edge, i.e., how can one verify that there
is a (u, v)-path? We focus on the second aspect and define the following certified shortcutting
procedure, in which the algorithm still gets (nondeterministic) advise on which shortcut edges
to add and also on paths that certify the validity of these edges, but forces the algorithm to
verify the path:
▶ Definition 3. A certified shortcutting procedure for a graph G starts with an empty
shortcut H and repeatedly takes some path P = (u1 , . . . , u|P | ) in the current graph G ∪ H,
verifies it using |P | steps, and then adds to H an arbitrary number of shortcut edges (ui , uj )
with i < j using one step per edge.
    We note that shortcut edges can be used in subsequent paths and therefore speed up future
verifications. For example, if one wants to shortcut two paths P and P ′ that share a long
subpath P ′′ , then they can be verified in |P ′′ | + (|P \ P ′′ | + 1) + (|P ′ \ P ′′ | + 1) = |P ∪ P ′ | + 2
steps by first adding an edge for P ′′ .
    We call an algorithm for directed reachability certified-shortcut-based if it first constructs
a shortcut H by a certified shortcutting procedure and then runs a breadth-first search on
G ∪ H. The first main result of this paper gives a stronger lower bound on the best depth
achievable by the certified-shortcut-based framework.
▶ Theorem 4. Any certified-shortcut-based algorithm for directed reachability with Õ(m)
work must have depth Ω̃(n1/4 ).

1.1.1      Certified Shortcuts: Definition and Equivalences
The key conceptual ingredient that powers the proof of Theorem 4 is a simple and natural
structural criterion, which captures shortcuts that can be easily verified and are therefore
more constructive in some sense.
▶ Definition 5. A shortcut H is certified if for any edge (u, v) ∈ H, there exist two edges
(u, w), (w, v) ∈ E ∪ H for some vertex w ∈ V .
   Being certifiable is a static structural property of a shortcut which is easy to state and
easy to (formally) argue about. One way to interpret this criterion is to think of it as a
requirement that every edge in H has two “parent” edges from which it could have been
derived. This induces a natural order in which any certified shortcut can be constructed via
a particularly simple certified shortcutting procedure that repeatedly shortcuts only paths of
length two. We call such a procedure a 2-hop certified shortcutting procedure.
▶ Lemma 6. Any shortcut H for a DAG is certified if and only if it can be constructed by a
2-hop certified shortcutting procedure.
Proof. Shortcuts constructed by 2-hop certified shortcutting procedures are certified by
definition. For the other direction, since H is a shortcut for a DAG G, G ∪ H is also a DAG.
Fix a topological order (v1 , v2 , . . . , vn ) of G ∪ H. Consider some shortcut edge (vi , vj ) ∈ H
certified by (vi , vk ), (vk , vj ) ∈ G ∪ H. It must hold that i < k < j, otherwise the topological
order would not be valid. Thus, a 2-hop certified shortcutting procedure can insert the edges
(vi , vj ) ∈ H in nondecreasing order of j − i, as j − i > max{j − k, k − i}.                      ◀

   A similar equivalence between general certified shortcutting procedures and certified
shortcuts holds, up to Õ(1) factors. In particular, one can transform any certified shortcutting
procedure into a 2-hop one with small overhead:

        ▶ Lemma 7. If a shortcut H for a DAG G can be constructed by a certified shortcutting
        procedure in t steps, then there exists a certified shortcut H ′ ⊇ H that can be constructed by

           The following corollary follows directly from the two lemma above.

        ▶ Corollary 8. If for a graph G, there does not exist a certified shortcut of size t that reduces
        the diameter to D, then any certified shortcutting procedure that reduces the diameter of G
        to at most D requires at least Ω̃(t) steps.

            On the other hand, if there exists a certified shortcut H of size t with diam(G ∪ H) ≤ D
        then there exists a simple (nondeterministic) 2-hop certified shortcutting procedure that takes
        t steps and reduces the diameter to D while also producing an easily and locally checkable
        certificate for the validity of H.


        1.1.2    Lower Bounds on Certified Shortcuts and Hopsets
        With the additional requirement of a shortcut being certified, we are able to prove stronger
        diameter lower bounds.

        ▶ Theorem 9. There exists a family of DAGs with n vertices and m edges, such that any
        certified shortcut of size Õ(m) has diameter Ω̃(n1/4 ).

            This theorem together with Corollary 8 completes the proof of Theorem 4. We remark
        that Theorem 9 can be easily derived from the constructions of [9, 11] and an improved
        alternation product due to [16].
            Our notion of certifiability also naturally extends to (exact) hopsets, which generalize
        shortcuts, by additionally requiring the weight of an added edge (u, v) to be equal to the
        total weights of its two certifying edges (u, w), (w, v). We similarly obtain improved lower
        bounds on hopbounds of certified hopsets.

        ▶ Theorem 10. There exists a family of unweighted undirected graphs with n vertices and m
        edges, such that any certified hopset of size Õ(m) has hopbound Ω̃(n1/3 ).

            To put this bound in context, we remark that existing hopset lower bound results had a
        gap between the cases of unweighted and weighted graphs. Though not explicitly stated, it
        appears that the lower bound of [5], combined with alternation products, implies a lower
        bound of Ω̃(n1/3 ) for the hopbound of Õ(m)-size hopsets in weighted graphs but left the
        case of unweighted graphs open. Subsequently, [10] proved a lower bound of Ω̃(n2/7 ) for
        unweighted graphs. The lower bounds in Theorem 10 proves the Ω̃(n1/3 ) bound for certified
        shortcuts in unweighted graphs.
            The discussion so far has focused on the setting where Õ(m) edges are added, which are
        the largest amount of edges any efficient algorithm can afford to add. For completeness, we
        also give lower bounds on certified shortcuts and hopsets with Õ(n) edges, even though these
        are less natural in the context of certified shortcuts.

        ▶ Theorem 11. There exists a family of DAGs with n vertices, such that any certified
        shortcut of size Õ(n) has diameter Ω̃(n1/3 ).

        ▶ Theorem 12. There exists a family of unweighted undirected graphs with n vertices, such
        that any certified hopset of size Õ(n) has hopbound Ω̃(n1/2 ).

1.1.3     Certification Complexity
As a final main contribution, this paper shows that one can use the concept of certified
shortcuts to define a complexity measure C(H, G) that gives some indication on how fast
one can hope to construct H. This complexity measure C(H, G) is purely structural, i.e.,
it does not involve and is independent of the procedure or algorithm that produced H.
It is also simple enough that it can be argued about formally. We believe this concrete
measure is a useful indicator and provides valuable guidance towards assessing whether any
given shortcut construction might have an efficient implementation. We give some evidence
for this belief by formally proving that our complexity measure perfectly predicts or at
least coincides with the current landscape of results on the efficiency of all known shortcut
constructions [19, 4, 7, 12, 14, 15, 2].
    Concretely, we define the certification complexity C(H, G) of a shortcut H in a DAG G
to be the smallest size of any certified shortcut H ′ in G that contains H:

▶ Definition 13. C(H, G) = min {|H ′ | | H ′ ⊇ H is a certified shortcut in G} .

     The name certification complexity comes from the following observation: A certified
shortcut H ′ that contains a given shortcut H can be seen as a natural and locally checkable
certificate for the validity of H. In particular, it suffices for any edge in a certified shortcut
H ′ to look at only its adjacent edges in G ∪ H ′ to detect a violation. The certification
complexity of a shortcut H is therefore exactly the size of the smallest locally checkable
certificate H ′ in this form that proves the validity of H.
     Alternatively, using the equivalences explained in Lemma 6 and Lemma 7, one can also
think of C(H, G) as exactly the number of steps a certified shortcutting procedure requires
to construct (a super set of) H, up Õ(1) factors.
     It is now natural to informally say that a shortcut H in a graph G is C-indicated to be
“efficiently constructible” if its certification complexity C(H, G) is comparable to the size of G
and C-indicated to be “not efficiently constructible” otherwise. Similarly, any (randomized)
shortcut construction, which given a graph G defines a shortcut H(G) (or a distribution over
such shortcuts), can be formally classified based on the complexity measure C as follows:
     We call a construction certified-shortcut efficient if for every graph G, the construction
(with high probability) produces shortcuts with certification complexity Õ(m). Conversely,
we call a construction provably certified-shortcut inefficient if there exists a family of graphs
such that the construction with high probability produces a shortcut with certification
complexity m1+Ω(1) for every graph in this family.
     We prove in Section 4 that this classification perfectly matches the state of the art
regarding what shortcut constructions have a known efficient implementation.

▶ Theorem 14 (Informal). Every known shortcut construction that has a known sequential/-
parallel algorithm with near-linear time/work [7, 12, 15, 2] is certified-shortcut efficient, i.e.,
provably always constructs shortcuts with certification complexity Õ(m).
   Conversely, every known shortcut construction for which no efficient implementation is
known, i.e., [19, 14, 4, 2], is provably certified-shortcut inefficient.

1.2     Prior Work
Shortcuts. The study of shortcuts dates back to [19], which provides a simple argument,
based on vertex sampling, showing the existence of O(n1/2 )-shortcuts of size Õ(n). This
folklore proof remains essentially the best known upper bound for decades, until a major
breakthrough due to [14] significantly improves the upper bound by constructing O(n1/3 )-
shortcuts of size Õ(n). Their result crucially relies on sampling of both vertices and paths.

            The use of random sampling is first avoided using greedy approaches in [4], which
        eliminates the logarithmic factors in the guarantees of [19]. Very recently, building upon
        this, [2] presents a similar improvement on the logarithmic factors over [14] also using greedy
        approaches. In fact, they further give a much more sophisticated analysis of [4] showing that
        it actually achieves the same guarantee of [14] up to logarithmic factors.
            Substantial effort has been made to speed up the computation of shortcuts. Specifically,
        improving upon [13], [15, 2] demonstrate almost-linear-time algorithms for computing O(n1/2 )-
        shortcuts using flow algorithms.
            In another concurrent line of work, [7] adapts the vertex-based approach of [19] and designs
        a work-efficient parallel algorithm for computing shortcuts in Õ(n2/3 ) depth. The depth and
        diameter bound is later improved to n1/2+o(1) by [12]. Unfortunately, it is unclear how to
        extend these frameworks to efficiently implement the path-based approach of [14]. In fact,
        assuming standard fine-grained complexity assumptions, any straightforward implementation
        would require strictly superlinear time even in the sequential setting [15].
            On the lower bound side, [9] constructs a family of layered DAGs, the diameter of which
        cannot be reduced below Ω(n1/17 ) by any O(m)-size shortcuts. In particular, it refutes
        a conjecture by [18] asserting the existence of linear-size shortcuts with polylogarithmic
        diameters for general graphs. Later on, [11] and subsequently [16] strengthen the diameter
        lower bound to Ω(n1/8 ) via better alternation products. All these constructions work with
        grid points in low dimensional Euclidean spaces and rely on a classical result by [3] which
        guarantees the existence of large convex sets. Currently, the state-of-the-art Ω(n2/9 ) lower
        bound is proved by [10] using new constructions without the use of such convex sets.
            Regarding O(n)-size shortcuts, the best known diameter lower bound is Ω̃(n1/4 ) due to [5],
        building upon [11]. [21] reproduces (and slightly improves by eliminating the logarithmic
        factors) the same result using constructions that later inspired [10].

        Hopsets. As hopsets are also shortcuts, all lower bounds for shortcuts naturally extend to
        hopsets. Additionally, [10] shows that no O(m)-size hopsets can reduce hopbounds below
        Ω(n2/7 ), an improvement over the Ω(n2/9 ) lower bound for shortcuts. The proof is by
        observing that uniqueness of shortest paths, rather than arbitrary paths, between critical
        pairs is sufficient.
            On the other hand, edge sets constructed by shortcut algorithms are not necessarily
        hopsets. In fact, the folklore sampling algorithm [19] and the original greedy approach [4]
        turn out to be essentially the only known shortcut algorithms, regardless of efficiency, that
        also produce hopsets. The same guarantee of O(n1/2 ) hopbound holds.
            It is also worth noting that for hopsets, whether or not the given graph is weighted also
        makes a difference, unlike in the case of shortcuts. While all aforementioned lower bound
        constructions are unweighted, [5] shows that [19, 4], which also work on weighted graphs, are
        essentially optimal for weighted graphs. Specifically, there exists a family of weighted graphs
        for which hopbounds cannot be reduced below Ω̃(n1/2 ) using any O(n)-size hopset. Though
        not explicitly stated, via alternation products, it also appears to imply an Ω̃(n1/3 ) hopbound
        lower bound for O(m)-size hopsets. Very recently, [2] proves that the greedy approach of [4]
        is existentially optimal in terms of both n and m for hopsets in weighted graphs.

    At a very high level, most known lower bound constructions for shortcuts are layered
graphs where each layer consists of integral grid points in constant (either 2 or 3 to be exact)
dimensions1 . The general goal is to pack as many long paths as possible into the graph such
that each path is the unique path between its endpoints and does not overlap too much with
other paths2 . Each such path is called a critical path and is defined by its starting vertex
and a critical direction, which specifies the exact edge to traverse in each layer.
    These constructions are typically parameterized by two numbers D and r. The depth
D corresponds to the number of layers in the graph, which is equivalent to the number of
edges in each critical path and thus should be maximized. Meanwhile, r typically controls
the range of the critical directions. In general, the goal is to pack a superlinear number of
critical paths so that no linear-size shortcut can reduce the length of every critical path.
Due to the layered nature of the graphs, the number of starting vertices is smaller than the
total number of vertices by a factor of D. This has to be compensated by the number of
critical directions, which is polynomial in r. As a result, it demands that r has a polynomial
dependency on D. To some extent, all later improvements can be viewed as optimizing this
relation between r and D via more complicated constructions.
    The most notable benefit of working with certified shortcuts is that such optimization is
no longer required. Indeed, in order to reduce the length of a critical path from D to D/2,
any certified shortcut has to add at least D/2 new edges. Consequently, we gain a factor of
Θ(D) for free, and it suffices to set r to be any large enough constant.
    It also seems plausible that our lower bounds are the best possible with current techniques.
Each layer needs to be at least 2-dimensional to allow for any nontrivial set of critical
directions, and an additional dimension is required for layering. This suggests the demand

         2     Preliminaries
        Notation. For n ∈ N, we use [n] to denote the set of integers {1, . . . , n}. ⟨·, ·⟩ denotes inner
        products. Bold letters are reserved for vectors.
            For r ≥ 0, let B(r) be the set of all 2-dimensional integral points within Euclidean distance
        r to the origin, and V(r) be the set of all vertices on the convex hull of B(r) and with positive
        coordinates. We use the following classical result by [3].

        ▶ Lemma 15 ([3]). It holds that |V(r)| = Θ(r2/3 ).

        Graphs. Given a (possibly weighted) graph G = (V, E), n = |V | and m = |E| are the
        number of vertices and edges respectively. The transitive closure of G is the set of vertex
        pairs (s, t) where s can reach t. For any path P , the length of P is the total weight of its
        edges, and we write |P | for the total number of its edges. For any two vertices s, t ∈ V , the
        distance from s to t, denoted distG (s, t), is the minimum length of any s-t path. We write
        distG (s, t) = ∞ if s cannot reach t. The subscript G is omitted when it is clear from context.
            A chain of a graph is a sequence of vertices (v1 , v2 , . . . ) such that vi can reach vi+1 for
        all i ≥ 1. An ℓ-chain cover is a collection of at most ℓ vertex-disjoint chains such that any
        path contains at most O(n/ℓ) vertices that are not in any chain.

        Shortcuts and hopsets. A shortcut with diameter D, or D-shortcut for short, is a set H of
        additional (unweighted) edges, such that for any two vertices s, t ∈ V ,
        1. If t is not reachable from s in G, then t remains unreachable from s in G ∪ H;
        2. If t is reachable from s in G, then t can be reached from s using at most D edges in
           G ∪ H.

           Similarly, an (exact) hopset with hopbound D, or D-hopset, is a set H of additional
